title: Readable in `print`, useless in a traceback
prompt: `Point` defines `__str__` and nothing else. `print` looks good; the REPL, a list of points and every traceback show the angle brackets.
hints: Which of the two falls back to the other when it is missing?

diagnose.silent: Nothing raised, and `repr` gave back the default `<Point object at 0x...>`. The fallback runs one way only: when `__str__` is missing, Python uses `__repr__`, but a missing `__repr__` has a default that nothing will ever tell you about. Since `__repr__` is what the REPL, a list of your objects, a debugger and every traceback show, writing only `__str__` means every place you actually need to identify an object shows a memory address. If you write one, write `__repr__`. Add `__str__` afterwards only when the output a program prints should read differently from the form that identifies the object.

tests:
p = Point(1, 2)
assert repr(p) == "Point(x=1, y=2)", f"repr gave {repr(p)}"
assert repr([p]) == "[Point(x=1, y=2)]"
assert f"{p}" == "Point(x=1, y=2)"

title: A representation you cannot read back
prompt: `User.__repr__` interpolates its fields plainly. A string field comes out bare, so the representation cannot be told from one holding a variable name.
hints: `f"{value}"` calls `str`. What should a `__repr__` call on its fields?
There is a conversion flag for it, and it is one character.

diagnose.silent: It runs, and `User(name=ada)` is ambiguous: nothing distinguishes a string from a bare name, and a nested object comes out in its `str` form rather than its own unambiguous one. The `!r` conversion in an f-string calls `repr` on the field, which quotes strings and recurses properly into anything that has its own `__repr__`. The goal a good `__repr__` aims at is that the output could be pasted back in to rebuild the object, and `!r` is most of what it takes to get there. It costs two characters per field and it is the difference between a debugging session that reads and one that guesses.

tests:
u = User("ada", ["admin"])
assert repr(u) == "User(name='ada', tags=['admin'])", f"repr gave {repr(u)}"
assert eval(repr(u)).name == "ada"

title: Refusing before asking the other side
prompt: `Money.__add__` raises when it does not recognise the other operand. Raising ends the operation; the other operand never gets its turn.
hints: There is a value a binary method returns to mean "I cannot do this, ask the other one".
Look at what `Coupon` defines, and work out what has to happen for it to be called.

diagnose.TypeError: `Money.__add__` raised, so the addition was over. `a + b` tries `type(a).__add__(a, b)` first, and if it returns the special value `NotImplemented`, Python then tries `type(b).__radd__(b, a)`. Raising skips that second chance entirely. Returning `NotImplemented` is not a fudge; it is the documented signal that lets a type you have never heard of cooperate with yours, and it is why `2 * vector` can work when `int` knows nothing about vectors. If nobody can do it, Python raises the `TypeError` itself, with a better message than yours, naming both types. Return the value, do not raise, and do not return `None`, which means something else entirely.

title: The cleanup that swallowed the error
prompt: `Timed.__exit__` records the elapsed time and returns `True`. A truthy return from `__exit__` suppresses the exception, so every failure inside the block disappears.
hints: What does the return value of `__exit__` mean?
The method has nothing useful to return. Say nothing.

diagnose.silent: Nothing raised, and that is the bug: an exception inside the `with` block was swallowed on the way out. `__exit__` returning a truthy value tells Python the exception has been handled and should not propagate, which is how `contextlib.suppress` is built and is almost never what a `__exit__` written for cleanup intends. Returning `True` because the cleanup succeeded is the natural mistake, and it turns a context manager into a blanket `except`. Return nothing. Python reads the implicit `None` as "I did not handle it", the exception carries on, and the cleanup still ran, because `__exit__` runs whatever happens.

tests:
t = Timed()
with t:
    pass
assert t.elapsed >= 0

failed = Timed()
try:
    with failed:
        raise ValueError("boom")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("the exception was swallowed on the way out")

assert hasattr(failed, "elapsed"), "the cleanup should still have run"

title: What `as` was given
prompt: `Session.__enter__` does its setup and returns nothing, so the name after `as` is bound to `None`.
hints: `with expr as name` binds whatever `__enter__` returns. What does this one return?
The object you want is almost always the one you already have.

diagnose.AttributeError: `__enter__` fell off the end and returned `None`, so `s` was `None` and the attribute access failed. `with expr as name` binds the **return value of `__enter__`**, not the object in the `with` statement, which is a distinction that only becomes visible when the two differ. Most context managers return `self`, and forgetting the `return` is the standard way to get a confusing `None`. The two are genuinely different sometimes, and that is the point of the design: `open()` returns a file, and a database connection's `__enter__` conventionally returns a transaction rather than the connection.

tests:
with Session() as s:
    s.calls.append("body")

assert s.calls == ["enter", "body", "exit"]

title: Cleanup that only happens when nothing goes wrong
prompt: `opened` yields in the middle of the function. The line after the `yield` runs on the way out, unless the body raises, in which case it never runs at all.
hints: The `yield` can raise. What construction makes the code after it run anyway?
This is the reason a context manager exists in the first place.

diagnose.silent: Nothing raised, and the cleanup was skipped for the one case that needed it. When the body of the `with` raises, `contextlib.contextmanager` throws that exception back in at the `yield`, so everything after it is skipped exactly as it would be in any other function. Wrapping the `yield` in `try`/`finally` is what makes the second half genuinely equivalent to `__exit__`, which runs whatever happens. Leaving it out is the standard bug in hand-written context managers, and it is a patient one: the code works for a year and leaks the first time something fails. If you want to see the exception rather than just clean up after it, `except` works there too, and re-raising afterwards is the default you want.

starter:
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def opened(log):
    """Record that a resource was opened, and close it on the way out."""
    log.append("open")
    yield log
    log.append("close")
tests:
clean = []
with opened(clean):
    clean.append("body")
assert clean == ["open", "body", "close"]

failed = []
try:
    with opened(failed):
        raise ValueError("boom")
except ValueError:
    pass
assert failed == ["open", "close"], f"the log ended as {failed}"

title: An empty answer read as no answer
prompt: `Result` defines `__len__`, which also decides its truthiness. A query that succeeded and matched nothing is therefore falsy, and reads as a failure.
hints: With no `__bool__`, what makes an object with `__len__` falsy?
Success and emptiness are different questions. Give the class a way to answer each.

diagnose.silent: It runs, and a query that worked perfectly and matched no rows was reported as a failure. Defining `__len__` also defines truthiness: an object without `__bool__` is falsy exactly when its length is zero. That coupling is convenient for lists and wrong for anything where "empty" and "absent" are different, which includes results, responses, and every wrapper that carries both a payload and a status. Define `__bool__` to answer the question you actually mean. The same trap is why `if some_dataframe:` and `if not response:` are so often bugs, and why the explicit `if len(x) == 0` is worth the extra characters when the object is not plainly a container.

tests:
assert report(Result([1, 2])) == "2 rows"
assert report(Result([], error="timeout")) == "the query failed"
assert report(Result([])) == "0 rows", f"an empty successful query reported {report(Result([]))!r}"

title: A protocol put on the instance
prompt: `Basket.__init__` attaches a `__len__` to each basket. Implicit dunder lookups go to the type, so nothing ever finds it.
hints: `len(x)` is not `x.__len__()`. Where does it look?
The method belongs somewhere that every basket shares.

diagnose.TypeError: `len(x)` is `type(x).__len__(x)`, so it searched the class, found nothing, and raised. Every implicit dunder lookup skips the instance: `repr`, `+`, `for`, `with`, all of them. This is not an oversight but a deliberate restriction, and it is the same one unit 20 met for descriptors. Looking `__repr__` up on the instance would mean every `repr()` call searched an instance dict first, and a class whose instances could each redefine `+` would be unreadable. It also means unit 19's `__getattr__`-answers-everything trap cannot accidentally make an object iterable or callable. Protocols go in the class body; per-instance behaviour goes in a plain attribute that the class's dunder reads.

tests:
b = Basket([1, 2, 3])
assert len(b) == 3
assert len(Basket([])) == 0
assert not Basket([]), "an empty basket should be falsy"
